figures.caption: Figure 2 | Key benefits of Experiment-as-Code labs. EaC translates scientific intent into standardized and reproducible specifications, enables safe and reliable execution, and supports scalable, efficient orchestration across shared, stateful laboratory resources.

Table 2 | Examples of device-specific control code and the corresponding EaC abstractions. EaC replaces low-level byte commands, serial I/O, parsing logic, and vendor-specific APIs with compact, typed operations that expose scientific intent while hiding device implementation details.

Figure 1 | The EaC framework bridges declarative experiment specifications and physical lab automation. EaC configs authored by scientists (1) are statically checked by the compiler against the lab state (2) and lowered into workflow DAGs (3). The scheduler consults lab state (4) to produce a state-aware execution plan (5), which the execution engine dispatches with runtime checks against live state (6, 7). The device interface translates unified operations into vendor-specific API calls (8), records returning telemetry (9), and refreshes the centralized lab state (10).

Figure 6 | Conductivity measurements for Li2SO4 aqueous electrolytes at varying concentrations. The experiment identifies 2.15 mol/kg as the highest-conductivity configuration under controlled conditions.

Figure 4 | The framework maintains a centralized representation of the laboratory state, including device availability, configuration, and runtime status. By tracking state transitions during execution, EaC enables safety checks and prevents conflicting or unsafe operations across devices.

Figure 3 | Example EaC configuration and its compiled execution graph. Declarative experiment steps are automatically expanded into device-level operations with inferred checks, dependencies, and teardown.

Figure 5 | Clio as a custom-built, small-scale proof-of-concept autonomous battery-lab platform. The platform integrates fluid-handling, measurement, actuation, and control devices within a compact heterogeneous workflow, demonstrating how EaC can standardize devices, coordinate multi-instrument procedures, and maintain shared lab state in a real laboratory deployment.
